speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm doing a recording today, July 1st, 1980, with Dorothy Anderson, who lives Potlatch Route 2 in Idaho. At first, we'll go through a personal data sheet, and then the idea is to go through the life history. As you said, this was done before, and it's been done as a resource on women's history in rural areas, because there's so little that's written about that. I'll ask some general questions about rural areas. Dorothy Anderson is your name, and your maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: McCroskey.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any nicknames?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I really never had. Well, if that was in college, Dot and Matt, but other than that, not now, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When were you born, and where?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: December 28th, 1927, in Great Falls, Montana.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm trying to make notes on these few things. Your husband's name is Sherrill, and that's H-E-R-R-S-H-E-R-R-E-L. When was he born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: March 4th, 1926.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right over home. He was born right on the place, so it's right here in the house over there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. I saw Anderson Farms, so probably this is his home place. Yeah, it's been in the family quite a while. And his occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's a farmer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And when were you born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was born in 1958.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: About the year?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 26, 19, it should be 58.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1958. Okay, we'll come back to her. What do you see as some of the advantages or disadvantages of living in a rural area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, let's see. We just came back from Los Angeles. A lot of advantages, I think, in living here. It seems like a smaller area of people, and you know so many of the people in the area. Of course, I know so many because I'm connected with teaching. So a lot of the students I've taught are still learning here. And I don't know, just a more helping attitude with people. If something goes wrong, like the years that we've had, wet years, and we've had a hard time getting crops harvested, you have, when some person finishes, they come to finish helping you. And I think neighbors you can rely on. I've never lived in the big cities, though, so I don't know. But I would think that it would be that, for one thing. Not the, there's just a feeling of rush to me when I get down into the cities, like LA and things like that. Traumatic. Yeah, that it just seems to be catching. It seems like everybody's in such a rush. Here, you don't seem to have that. I think also you have a big area to pick from for entertainment. We can still go to Spokane for some things, and McMaster and Coleman Close. And we're still close to camping facilities and things like that. I like the smaller school, too, to raise Sue. There were disadvantages, I felt, because she couldn't have all the classes. I wish she could have had, but at the same time, it was a much more personal, good to know everybody.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: More helpful. And friendly atmosphere. You've really been comparing the life, somewhat, of the rural woman, but would you make any other comparisons between the life of the rural woman and the urban woman? Hmm. And the friendliness you mentioned. Yeah, and the closeness of people.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. You know, it's kind of hard anymore. I think your rural woman's life is quite different than what it used to be. I went to school in Nebraska and left there, taught there, and no way was I going to stay there because everybody was farmers,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: and I wasn't going to marry a farmer.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was not going to stop on a farm. But here it seems different. You're so close to town, you don't feel isolated.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you feel like you have some of the advantages of being both rural and close to a more urban area.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Kind of confined here during harvest is about the only thing I can say. But now when we don't even hire to work, I can leave even during harvest for the day. So one time maybe I'd leave my husband a sandwich. Other than that, he's the kind of guy that fixes for himself. So I've never felt tied down.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you don't really have any feeding responsibilities or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Even during harvest now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they did at one time when we would hire outsiders to come in maybe and help a little bit. But with all this equipment today, one or two can do the whole thing. We have just about a 300-acre farm, so it's a smaller farm. I think at one time, when we were first marrying out here, I kind of felt obligated to fix chickens and to do a lot of canning. Although I enjoyed it at the time. It didn't seem too bad, except I didn't enjoy fixing chickens and taking care of chickens. And I never did. I never did learn to like that. But today, we don't do that anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, did you live on a farm when you were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I lived in a small smelting town, and I suppose there was about 13,000.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was going to ask how you would compare your family life when you were growing up with family life now.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think I like the family life we've had here on the farm. I think Cheryl has been closer to our daughter Sue than what my dad was when he was working. He had his regular work hours, and just with his two weeks vacation, and we would see him, of course, at dinner, and that would be where we had the closest. I think we've had here, where Cheryl was fairly free in the wintertime, and when Sue was little, she was sick, he was the one that would take care of her, because I taught. It seems family life, I really like it better than I did in town. Our playground was the street, and of course here, the kids have a lot more to do. I think on the farm, I notice the kids in school are always, it's the town kids that dread the first few weeks until the swimming pool opens and that, while the country kids are really anxious, and they have a lot of things to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You indicated that you haven't always lived in Idaho. When did you come to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I came in 1948, and I came here to teach.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you came to Potlatch to teach in 1948? And did you have a car at the time that you drove here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no car. I didn't even know how to drive until after we were married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So how did you get to Potlatch?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you would, it was usually people would bring you up here. Or we'd get to Moscow to catch a bus. Yes, I had Aunt Rutland Lewiston, and my cousin came to teach with me here, so they'd come back and forth. Or people around here would see that we got to Moscow to catch a bus.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But did you come from your home in Montana?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I had been teaching a year in Nebraska. So I had gone home after I had taught that year, and then I had gone to Lewiston to visit relatives for this part of the summer. And I was there when I decided to make a change.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, now looking back to your teaching, but if we look even farther back, did you know your grandparents?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, my mother's parents. I never did know my father's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did they live?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Lewiston, Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you had some acquaintance with this area before?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, Lewiston. Not up here, but yes, I did live in Lewiston area.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This general area. And what was your grandfather's occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He worked at the mill.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that was their community. And now your parents. I'd like to get actually their names and ages and birthplaces. Your mother?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They are both dead. My mother was Florence Wolfe McCroskey. She was born in 1899. I know that because she was always in New York. That's wrong. And my dad was Nathan. Oh, boy, you know, I can't remember. Okay, he was about six years older than my mother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, about 93 or something like that. And they're both dead, you said. Do you recall when they died?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My mother died just, let's see, three years ago. My dad must have died about six years ago.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And, you know, were they born in Lewiston?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. My dad was born in Kentucky and my mother was born in Lewiston.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know when they were married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I can't remember the dates. I've looked it up one time, but I'm not one much to remember dates. I'm trying to think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have sisters and brothers?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have one sister and one brother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And their names?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My sister is Alice. And her name is Sharpe. I do need that. And my brother's name is Burke.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And their approximate ages?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All right, my sister's 42. And my brother is four years younger than I am, so he'd be...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He'd be 48. He was born in 1932, I think. Okay, and when did you come to Idaho? When did you come to Lewiston?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I came and teach in 1938, but we would come to Lewiston in the summer times with Mother to visit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you came to Lewiston in 1938 and then you lived here continuously?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it was 1948 that I first came to teach here. You mean permanently started to live? Then you'd have to put 48, because the other times we were in Lewiston was just to visit and not for the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you came to visit, would you mostly drive?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we took the train. My folks did not have a car and we took the train.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, now, let's... How would you... What would you describe your parents' life? Where did they live?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They lived in Anaconda, and it was a smelting town. It seemed like Dad worked, and his whole life was his work. He took his vacation at Christmas times, so we never went on vacations as a family. It was Mother and us kids would come to Lewiston to visit. But that was about the extent of any vacations. In the early years, it was the smelting town, they always seemed to be on strike, and of course it was kind of a bad time anyway. And so we didn't have a lot of extras. I never remember going without anything, you know, having to skimp or anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean the Depression years, you're remembering.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, and it really wasn't, I don't think, until the beginning of the Second World War that things started to boom for the smelting, and they seemed to have a little bit more. But they stayed pretty close to home. Mother was active in outside things through the day, but she was always home at night then. Our whole life was just kind of centered right there in Anaconda, we never really went very far. We had the hills close to us, and we'd do a lot of climbing the hills, and I said, playing in the streets, that was our baseball field.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Can you think of other things that you and your brothers and sisters did?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We didn't do much together as a family. Our age difference there, four years and ten years now, doesn't make any difference, but then it did, and you didn't. The little sister, you know, it's fun to take her around, but you're glad to get rid of her, and the brother was just enough that you kind of clashed in most everything you did. So, at home we did a lot of, we played games. Friday night was kind of the night we listened to radio, and it was the night Dad bowled, he did bowl, and we'd, it was kind of a special night, mom popcorn, and we'd play games and things like that. I think we did, my brother and I did a lot of, oh, playing Monopoly and different games like that. You know, he was young, I can remember playing soldiers with him, with all his lead soldiers that he had. But, that was probably about the extent of it. And then I started to work when I was a freshman in high school, and I would work from the time I'd get home from school, until ten at night in a little corner grocery store about just a block from home, and then I would close up. And you'd hear I'd be the only one there unless someone would come in to put the money away or something. But, so, even in high school I didn't take an active part in some of the things that the kids would do today, in some of the sports and that, although there weren't a lot of sports activities like you have today.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you mention coming to visit your grandparents in Lewiston? Are there reunions or weddings or holiday celebrations or deaths, you know, that you remember?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it was mainly just, I think about once every four years, that was about what could be afforded. I think it was never said, but I think they figured that. And we usually stayed quite a while, a month or longer, I suppose, that I always thought, well, if you're that much for tickets, well, you might as well, you better stay a while. And it was, yeah, when we would come, and then, of course, my grandparents, my aunt lived there, and then later I had another aunt that, and her family lived there. So it was the picnics in the parks, a lot of picnics, and things like that. And my grandmother was great for, she liked to cook, and of course she felt that's what women should do. She worried about me when I was married and still teaching how in the world I was going to put a meal on the table, you know, because I didn't do most of it. But she always set just a beautiful table, regardless of whether she was eating by herself or with all of us, she had things out that sometimes we put aside to do, and do it while the good things were out. But we did a lot of, yeah, we did that. And it'd be just the family getting together.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have other family around where you were living?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we didn't. And I think that's why we didn't have the family celebrations, having family in.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You said that you worked during high school. Did you and your brother and sister have responsibilities in your home? Chores that you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it was, any chores we had were usually connected with cleaning our room. We all helped, like get meals and do dishes, helped with the washing, dragging in and out that old washing machine, and things like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, ringer washing machine. Yeah, the old ringer machine. Who would you say was responsible for the discipline in your family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think probably, well, both of them, but I think Dad. When Dad spoke, we never argued. With Mother, we would argue a little bit with her. So she was much more lenient. But I think most of it fell on her shoulders until Mom and Dad would take over sometimes. And he was the kind that when he said something, you did it right then, you didn't hear it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, how would... and then he was the authority. I was going to ask how he would describe the attitude towards women on his part, or on the part of your mother.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, Mother was very free to take part in like her different, the clubs she belonged to and her church organization and that. But of course she didn't go at night, and that could have been because we didn't have a car. It was difficult to go in place at night, unless someone would pick you up. And she kind of felt she should be home at night, I suppose. But on the other hand, she always, Dad never, you know, she could go. And later years, when he retired, they moved to Moscow. She didn't worry about, you know, if she was going to be gone to fix him his dinner. He could get along. He fixed his own meals and that. So he was quite handy that way, and it was a clean house. I was always used to, you know, Dad would do things like that. So it was never... Mother was the only one who could do that. Dad did it too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The vision of labor wasn't hard and fast.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. And when it came time for school, to go away to college, they really didn't have many of the, all the guidance counselors like they have today. They were beginning to have some that would kind of steer you. And I remember one trying to talk to me and said that I would probably be better if I, you know, would just find a good job in a store there and be happy to stay there. And I said, well, I was going to college. And I think they felt my folks couldn't afford it. And tried to steer me to something else, which really irritated Dad to no end.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because he wanted to be all educated. Did your parents expect you to go to college?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Because I came home and said one time, maybe it would be better if I waited a year and worked. And Dad didn't like that at all. He paid for two years of college for me. And then I realized my brother would be coming up. And at that time you could go out and teach on two years very easily. And so I realized two years was enough and I could go out and teach. I did the rest on my own. But, yes, he was very... School was, you know, education was important to him. He hadn't had education. My mother had had a couple years of college, but my dad hadn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He wanted your brother and sister also then to go to school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. They all did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they did better in college.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Bert went to school for a couple years. Then, of course, the Korean War came along. And he was four years in the Navy. And then he came back and did the rest on his own, too. And my sister had all four of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You said your mother had several years of college. Did she teach?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, she taught.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What would you describe as some of your... Let's see. First of all, I guess I want to ask, you said you went to school for two years. Where did you go to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: University of Nebraska-Lincoln. And I think I went there... I had had... Anaconda was very much a union town. You didn't do anything without belonging to the union. When I was in high school, I had to belong. Because I worked, even though it was part-time. And when I first belonged, they said, well, you can't work after six. Well, that ruined everything for me. Well, it just so happened the man that owned the store was called into the Army. So I was able to work at night, because, you see, he wasn't there. And someone could work. But I'd had some unhappy experiences with him, it seemed. I wanted to get clear away from Montana. And, of course, my mother had gone to Nebraska. So that's why.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did you have some relatives in Nebraska at the time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: None that I knew. I think there were some around Benkelman. But they had been gone so long.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Had she gone to the University of Nebraska also? That's interesting. And then did you go on to school after you taught?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Then after I moved up to Potlatch, and I went to summer schools with my mother for two years. And then after Sue was born, I quit teaching for six years, or five years. And then that sixth year, before she went back to school, I went back and got my master's degree. And then I keep, you know, I just am in between my master's and my sixth year. I'm in college, so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You went to Nebraska, and then you got your bachelor's from the University of Idaho? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I got my master's from the University of Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you got your master's from... What would you say were some of your special skills or interests?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Let's see, now do you mean other than teaching?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, teaching.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay, well, teaching, yes, definitely.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you a reading teacher? Yes, I am.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Reading and English.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You worked, and then you said your first job was a part-time job when you were in high school. Clerk in the grocery store. Did you work while you were in college, too? No, I didn't.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I didn't work those two years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you said you taught for... Did you say you taught one year at Lewiston?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I taught one year in Venango, Nebraska.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, in Nebraska.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Then I came up to Potlatch, and I've been here ever since.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And so you taught for a while before you were married. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, from 48 to 52, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you say you spent your leisure time then? What groups had you been involved in while you were teaching? Oh, you mean when I was going... While you were still single.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, of course, in college it was... I don't know what it was with the college functions that were on, games.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sports events.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The games put on. The dances, the games put on. Going home with, you know, the students we met. We did quite a bit of that. And got a taste. That was my first taste of farm life when I went home with a girl. In Nebraska, I think. But they didn't have electricity, and we had the outhouse that I had never been used to. And then when I came up here, I think it's... Oh, dances. I went to Spokane to different functions that would come along. What kind of functions? Your circuses, your... I don't know if there's any special musical groups that might come. I can remember seeing a banjo player, Peabody, I think it was, that I was very impressed with. Plays. Going to the plays, you know, both places. You do a lot of visiting at people's houses, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you live in Potlatch?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I lived right in Potlatch. At that time, see, Potlatch, when I first came here, was owned by the lumber company. The town was owned by them. But the board just kept a house. They just kept a house for teachers. And it was all furnished. And each bedroom had two. Everybody had their own bed, their own dresser, their own... their own desk. You had to clean your week, and you had to cook for night meals, and have things there for breakfast and lunches for them to fix. And you pooled. I mean, you just, all the bills went in. What brought us here is because it was one of the cheaper places. It was quite reasonable to live up there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And this was provided for single teachers?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, just single teachers. Almost like a cooperative. Yeah, and so we did things together. I learned a niche, you know, with the group. So a lot of wintertime.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Social activities probably centered around that house.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we played pinochle and maybe had others. One time we had other teachers come in. It was... you were connecting with the people that you worked with. To a smaller extent. It wasn't as much then when I was single. We weren't really included. I can't say really with the teachers at that year either. They didn't include the single teachers at that time. The married ones had their own little groups. And so the few single ones there...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Single ones. And of course... Get together, some connection with living together.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And probably all of our entertainment, we went to Moscow, or we went to Skokien, or we went to Kordulia.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And somebody had a car.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, usually the fellow, you know, wherever you're going with that. Transportation.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well that sort of leans into courtship and marriage. What are some of the things that you remember about your courtship and early marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I met Cheryl through... Well, let's see, it's his brother's wife now. She was a home ec teacher there and she was going with his brother. This one time they decided they wanted to have a steak dinner and invite the fellows they were going with. My cousin had come up here to teach and she was going with the grade school principal. And I usually went to Lewiston. The kid that I was going with at the time had gone on back to Chicago and was going to school back there. And so I sort of didn't have any study at the time, so they taught me to stay. And Cheryl had just come from California. He'd been going to school down there. And so that's how I met him. I really reluctantly stayed. I didn't want to, but I did. He was around a lot. He came up a lot if it wasn't just to... just to come up to see me for the evening. And of course he'd come up and visit. He was there with all the other teachers too, you know. It was just one big group that'd be there in the living room, you know. But it seemed to be alright. And he had the car, so I probably saw more of the country then because we went different places in New York and Yugota. When it was nice, you'd go to see different, you know, points of interest around. Went to dances a lot. Went to the Oaks Club a lot to their dances.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In Moscow and so...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it was one of the main places, I guess, for their dances and eating out and things like that. Took in a lot of the university functions, I mean games and things like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you expect, always sort of expect to get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you feel that your mother expected you to get married? No. No, I don't mean married, you know, specifically to Cheryl, but just that this would be what you would do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't think there was anything like, you know, you just get married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So there were other options, you feel?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yes. I mean, it was just a... Yeah, I never felt that, you know, marriage was it. They never really talked about it too much. There was one kid I was going with, Seriously, and I think they were a little worried I might marry him because I don't think they liked him as well. But, it was never, you know...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But they got you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And when I first started going with Cheryl, it definitely wasn't... You know, it was a...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your family get to meet him then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We went together about four years before we met. Yes, he... Of course, I would be going to summer school, so I wouldn't be home very much, but I'd go home as soon as school was out, and then he came over and... After me one time, he stayed a couple days. So yes, they met him even before we were serious in that sense. And...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Can you remember any particular things about your early married life? Did you, when you got married then, did you live here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we lived in Moscow. He wasn't farming, he worked at the Chevrolet garage over there. And we lived in Moscow a couple years, so I commuted. And since I didn't drive, there were others who commuted, and then I paid my share and went back and forth. And... I think probably then, with the entertainment... We went to the show a lot. TV was just coming in, but... TV didn't interest us. And I don't think at the time we really thought we could afford a TV, but we went to shows a lot, and we had friends we would go visit. And I know at Christmas, one year, he worked, so we didn't get home Christmas to my home. And we always celebrated Christmas Eve in my house. And his family, it was always Christmas Day, so we would come out here for Christmas Day with his friends, while we fixed up gifts for their kids, because they had some little kids, and several Christmas Eves went there, just so that I could have a Christmas Eve. But again, it was me and him being... at people's houses, with personal friends.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And a lot of times, those that had children... Did a number of the people who you had taught with, in your part-lives, the single teachers, or even then the couples, were they personal friends?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, then it was more the friends he'd made after we were married, I think. Those I had taught with sort of... Some of the single ones had moved away, and we would see his brother and wife a little bit, because they were having children, and they had little ones, and didn't get out very much, and we'd go over and see them occasionally. And then my cousin, they moved away, so it was mainly then, I think, the people he had met. And it wasn't... We didn't really get in much with teachers until we actually moved over here then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In Moscow, so we were that far removed, from the evenings and weekends from part-life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we got over to see his folks a lot. And we did a lot of things with his folks when we were here. There was a lot of peanut-cooking with him over the evening, or the day.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you remember any particular... old preparation that you had for childbirth, or for other feminine things, like periods or things like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Um... Mom had, right now with my aunt, they took both my cousin and I and... explained everything, and had books and things like that. So I wasn't in the dark with things like that. I don't think Mom seemed to cover things quite well. I don't know... Maybe not so much preparation for marriage, you might say. But there was no... Anything I ever wanted to ask, I asked, I think, and had an answer to. And then... Sue was born. It seemed like everything had been quite well explained.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You said that Sue was born in Moscow, and so you had medical services there. Were you still living in Moscow at the time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we were out here in the barracks.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Not that far away. So you had the medical services there. She was born in Gritman?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we had a doctor in Potlatch at the time. My husband had a plane at that time, and we had an airstrip out in the back, and there were three in it, and the doctor was in on it. But I had gone to this doctor in Moscow, and I still felt more at ease with him. But this one came in every night from here, talked to me and stuff. We still went up there to him and all those things, but I did go to this doctor in Moscow. It was the one we'd gone to all the time, but when we first moved over there, I felt more at ease with him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You didn't come from a large family? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And even Cheryl, who just has one sister and one brother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think there are any particular factors that affected having one child yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, well...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you want more children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. When we were first married, I think children were the farthest from our mind. At the time, we didn't want to start having a family right away, and we didn't. We enjoyed the freedom we had. On a weekend, if we just decided, let's drive up to Canada, you could. You didn't have to worry about it. I think then we finally realized, I was 30 when Sue was born, and if we were going to have one, we better think about it. And then I think because of our age at the time, we decided we'd just end up with a woman. I think maybe it was because we started later. Probably for her, she had a brother or sister, someone else, as I'm closer to my brother and sister now than I used to be at that time. At that time, it seemed to be... that was going to be it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was going to ask how you then spent your time after Sue was born. You said that Cheryl had more time for her. You had taught up until the time she was born.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, and then I didn't teach then, after she was born. I taught for six years. We were a little more confined to home then, but we were ready for it. It didn't bother us to have to stay home, you know, Saturday nights when you usually would go out and do something. So we did a lot more things here at home, and probably did more things with family. And then it was shortly after that my folks moved to Moscow. And then my sister came to Moscow to go to school. She was still going to college. My brother ended up then, after a few years, in Moscow too. He was in the architect department. He's still with the University of Idaho, but not in that department anymore. So now I had family closer. So now we began to have the family get-togethers on my side. Where we did a lot of... we'd go to your house, we'd come to ours, with all of us, with kids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Celebrating holidays together.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, definitely. Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter are the main ones. Didn't always get together for the birthdays celebration. Occasionally we would. Now my mother's, we would. We always did things with Mom and Dad for their birthdays or something like that. We'd get together for those, but not necessarily for all of ours. But really, when you start to think about it, did a lot with family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. You had the larger family right around you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. So now, and then with my aunt, she would come up, you know, for different celebrations, and we would go down.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You had your husband's family, and then your parents.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We seemed to do more with my family than he did with his family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: After they moved here, you did a lot more with them. Mm-hmm. Did, what magazines do you take? Or do you watch TV programs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: TV has, we watch TV, but it's never been our, you know, main thing. And we never had the problem with our daughter gluing, taking her with, that she'd be glued to the TV. Never had that problem. And as she was in school and that, she had her own room. We'd go there a lot to do her practicing or her homework. There were kind of special programs we liked to watch. If there wasn't a program on, and even now, if there isn't something that sounds interesting, we don't even bother to turn it on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you say you're more readers?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we're all readers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I asked the question about magazines, and then I passed over it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we take a lot of magazines. I take McCall's and Better Homes and Gardens, Changing Times, National Geographic, have taken, oh, the Smithsonian Magazine. Just dropped it last year. Didn't realize we had dropped it. It was kind of a mistake, but I thought we had it and didn't, and I've never renewed it again. Newsweek, and Time Magazine. I take papers. We lost a lot of them. We take two papers, and his folks take two others, and then we switch, so we have...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you all do a lot of reading? Yes. You and your husband?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sue, do a lot of reading herself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, she did a lot, and she was a very good reader. And we all do a lot of reading. We have to go to bed, too, and read through the day. And I do a lot. I do handwork. There's certain things that, if I'm going to watch TV, I can't just sit down. I have some knitting going or some crocheting, and Sue, I noticed, she's into the macramé and hook rugs and things like that, so she does a lot of sewing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever entered any of these in any of the county fairs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I haven't. I've thought about it, but I just... You've been working there? The last time we went over there, I thought, oh, I should enter some of the sweaters I do, that I have done, so... But I always think about it too late, and I thought, well, next year I might just... I finished Cheryl's sweater this year, but it turned out... Oh, that's nice. I thought pretty well I'd do that. Oh, well, all the... Is that what you do especially? Knitting? Yes, it has been the knitting that I've enjoyed. You've done a lot of sweaters and things? Yes, but it's probably been in the later years. When Sue was littler, I guess I knit her a few sweaters, and I did some sewing out of necessity, because I wasn't teaching, and we were just taking her to the farm, and money was pretty tight. So I did learn to sew, but I enjoyed it then, but when she got about junior high age, she started to sew, and then she just did her own sewing from there on, and made most of her own clothes. So I kind of quit sewing and went into the other, so the knitting of that has been, you know, maybe even later.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that your...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The main...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What shall I say? Skill like embroidery or... Yes, I...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I... No, I have a potter's wheel and a kiln, but for some reason I've let it slide, and haven't done anything for several years with it, but I took a class up at school, the art teacher taught a class in pottery, and really liked it, so she got me the kiln and the potter's wheel. So, no, I do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you have some other crafts?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, and I make candles. I like to make candles, and do a lot of that, especially around Christmas time, and usually in the summer I make my candles for Christmas. So I guess those, yeah, those crafts. I like to be outside in the garden. I kind of went flowers first, and now I've kind of gone the other way. I've gone back to the vegetable garden, had several years when I didn't bother with the vegetable garden, and didn't see any trouble, but now I kind of like, I don't do a lot of canning of it like I used to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you, like the years when you were at home, after Sue was born, did you do a lot of canning?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Yes, I do. Well, when we first moved out here, his folks always had a huge garden, and so I just felt, this is what I should be doing, you know, so I got into the garden work and into the canning, and we would go down and pick our fruit on, it wasn't too far where we went, it was down here, where we called it, Rawa'i, I think. It's all flooded now. But yeah, we went down, but Cheryl would go too, to pick the fruit. He always helped pick the fruit, and then I'd come back and can it, and we ate a lot of it at that time, it seemed, we had a lot of fruit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you canned it, did you do any freezing? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I didn't, but when we first started, I didn't have a freezer, but we had a locker box in Palouse, and then the folks, when we moved out here, we bought a freezer together, and the big one, she had her upright too. So yes, I've always had the freezer, so we've done a lot of freezing, and we had our own meat until, well, it's been a number of years, but we still buy a fourth of a beef or half a beef now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: These are things that Cheryl's parents did, and your mother did here. And did your, after your, I suppose when your parents moved to Moscow, your father retired, did your mother ever do any canning too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You said your grandmother liked to cook now,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: did she? Oh yes, grandma, they would go over to Clarkston and pick the fruit, and had the gardens and canned, yes. Always did a lot of canning.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But now, you say that that has changed,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: and now you're self.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you said in gardening, you have sort of gotten back into it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, into the gardening now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Some vegetables.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's kind of one way to get outside, and it's to have to eat during the summer, but I really, well, I'll freeze some things if I have another supply for you, but I will have squash for the winter that I just put in the cellar and things like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you don't get any fruit now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we don't. We don't go pick the fruit. And I guess we finally decided when I took a look at it, you know, by the time you buy the fruit and everything, I finally decided I wasn't saving very much. And it was always kind of a rush just before school started to be canning. I kind of lost interest, I think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's a lot of that comes at the end of the summer, just as the teaching responsibilities really.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we found we could survive without having the fruit, and I think as you get older you decide, well, you know, we don't really need all of that. I'm sure I cooked differently than what his mother did. I mean, we don't have the three big meals a day. And, you know, cut back, and we survived. I have to laugh because Cheryl loves the salad. He'll like a shrimp or tuna salad at night, even during harvest. And his mother, well, you don't have anything hot,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: you know, quite a change.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, so I see that with some of them that, you know, you don't have dessert, but we just very seldom have dessert.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And of course you weren't home at noon when you were teaching.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, and when I first went to teaching I would try and leave a sandwich, and that didn't last very long. He said, gee, I don't need that. A lot of noons I don't want that sandwich. If I'm not working hard, I don't need it. So I don't leave anything anymore. It just gets long gone.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did you have to make any special arrangements when you went back to teach? Or Sue was in school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was, see, I didn't go back to teach until she was ready for school. Now I did go back to the university and went that whole year, but she went to kindergarten, Presbyterian kindergarten, and just had to walk a block to my folks' and they kept picking them up until I would come in the afternoon to pick her up. And it worked out very handy. Yes, it was nice. She got to kind of know her grandparents a little bit more by being with them so much, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you always plan to teach even before you went to college?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I think that was the only thing that was ever in my mind. I don't know if maybe it was the fact that there didn't seem to be too many things open to you. And of course my mother taught and my two aunts had taught, and it just sort of seemed the natural thing to do. Natural job for a woman. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you think you would continue to teach after you got married? When you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, when we got married I knew I was going to go on to teach.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you were interested in getting back to it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I think when Sue was little I got involved in a lot of other activities. And then I was on school board for six years, too, that I was not teaching. But I finally decided I was just as organized, more organized when I taught than when I was home here. And really I got so busy that it didn't even seem like I sometimes had time for anything around the house with the outside organizations. And I thought, well, gosh, teaching, I'll be more relaxed or I won't be on the go so much. It wasn't when I went back that the money was needed at that time. But you enjoyed it,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: especially enjoying teaching. Yeah, I enjoyed it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I just didn't think I could, just being with Sue in school and just being around home, I didn't think enough for me to do it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you've been on the school board and you've been involved in other community activities at that time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was Eastern Star and had been worthy majoring and we've always been involved with church and I had an office there. And then our women's association, the church women's association, and had offices there. And of course, it's like everything else, when I wasn't teaching, Dorothy doesn't work, she can do this, you know. And then I had Sunday school classes and then they had their little, oh, their rural clubs that they had here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then they had their garden clubs or homemaker clubs.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, homemaker clubs and that. And of course, I got involved, when I wasn't teaching, I got involved with that and enjoyed that. And it was an entirely different group of people that I'd never been around before, but they were still the community people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were they women in like in this immediate area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, they were.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were these sponsored by home ec demonstration?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think it is kind of a home demonstration thing and it's all connected, I think, with your 4-H. I think they still, from Moscow, the extension service comes out with different things. And they had very interesting programs and things like that that I enjoyed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, you said that you have been involved in church too, so church and religion you would consider important.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Presbyterian. In Potlow. Have you continued these community activities, any of these community activities after you started teaching again?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Church, well, I dropped out of the women's group they meet during the day. A lot of these meet during the day. I think Eastern Star, I've kind of dropped, I don't go to it all the time now, it's Thursday nights and it seems like as Sue was growing up, and especially in high school, we became so involved. We were still very involved in school functions. I think in this community a lot of your social work is involved around the school, what's going on at school, when they have their school plays and their games, their band concerts and that. I think a lot of people take those in in organizations when they're making money.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Social activities for parents.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And Sue was so involved with everything and we tried, we went. The times that we thought, she said, well, you mean neither of you are coming? And so we just always went. And that began to take so much of our evening time that I sort of dropped out of Eastern Star, I'm still a member, but I wasn't as active in that. But I still am, we still are with the church, but I don't have a Sunday school class anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But now that speaks about some of your family activities as she got older and was in high school and did quite a lot of things with her or attended things that she was involved in. Was she in sports?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, and band. Drama? No, not drama, but she was in band and sports. And of course she was in all the sports, it seemed. And any functions, dinners or anything they were putting on, of course she went. She was in the National Honor Society, so anything they did, we went also. And we chaperoned a lot of the dances and that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you say that the school is really a social center of the community?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I think it is, and I think it probably still is even with SUPON, because we don't feel like we have to go to quite so many games. But you see, I'm in junior high, so I kind of feel obligated to go to junior high functions, the games and that. And we enjoy going to high school games, and there's the girls' high school game, and there's the boys' and there's the volleyball games and basketball and football. Yes, I think we are very much so. Now, though, we do belong to a bridge club that we enjoy, and it's once a month and it's their couples. And I belong to a women's bridge club and I do go to that. And it's not entirely made up of girls. It's not made up of teachers. It's other people in the community. And Cheryl, I don't see what group did he belong to. He was kind of slack on that. I'd go sometimes for husband and wife and that is a kind of a community. It's like a JC's, but it wasn't JC's either. Lions Club.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, mm-hmm. And there's ladies' lines, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They don't have a ladies' lines. I think they're going to start one up there, but for this time I said, you know, you get so many nights and so you sort of...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think the role of children has changed since Sue was young? And maybe sort of coupled with that I was going to ask, do you see changes in your role as teacher? You had a period of time, actually, of course, when you taught before she was born.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I see a change in this community with the kids coming in. I sometimes feel that they don't give the kids enough responsibility. They don't know how to do things maybe on their own. I'm seeing more of that. My mother does more of the things and I don't know why.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think that's true for both the children in town and the children in the rural area? You mentioned that you felt that...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think those in town have less. The children in the rural areas are doing a lot more. I have more responsibility. A lot of ours belong to 4-H and have animals to take care of and things like that. The ones in town seem to have less to do. I see the... kind of a breakdown in respect. And maybe it's... I find if you show them respect they'll try and show back. But it's the ones that do a lot of moving around. The ones that have problems. I see different types of problems. I don't know if I'm getting older...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you think this has developed increased a lot in the more recent years that you've been teaching?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: To a certain extent, yes. I don't think it's all... the respect part... I don't think it's all bad. It used to be we would have... you must dress this way. You had no choice. And I've been through the change of that and I think, why do the girls always have to wear dresses? And I see the kids wanting to... that way, wanting to take more of what they're going to do I think, with themselves. And I still say, like the dress code and that still should be... the parents should decide. But it's a good out if you can say, well, I'd like school to do it because I want my kids

speaker: Speaker 1
words: to go to high school about three years ago.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Seventy-six.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Seventy-four years ago. Had there been a change then to this more flexible or has that sort of come since you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh no, this was before she... Well, she was in high school. Well, she was down... when we dropped her dress code she was down to say junior high, grade school and all this turmoil.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: After she graduated from high school

speaker: Speaker 2
words: she went to college. She went three years to the University of Idaho and then she was married last year and she finished over in... they live in Olympia and she finished at a... it was a private Catholic college at Lacey.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So at St. Martin's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, St. Martin's. She finished in accounting. She apologized when she started that she didn't want to go into teaching. She went into engineering but she didn't... I think it was as exciting as she was. She was a BS in accounting. Yeah, she's an accounting. I'm not sure that she was...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think she was a BS.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think she was a BS.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they live over there in that area. We talked about... some of the changes. Since you've been a teacher as far as the children, have you changed in what you've taught or things like this? Have you always been a reading teacher?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I started out fifth grade and then I moved up to junior high. And yes, I've been mainly connected to language arts.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that's been a special interest. Uh-huh. And I was going to ask about recreation and relaxation. You talked about the different crafts that you do. Do you... people go camping? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We had a camp on a pickup and now we have a trailer. And at first you said

speaker: Speaker 1
words: you do things with the school but what else would you... or what do you do? What camping do you do

speaker: Speaker 2
words: or what else would you describe as your leisure activities? Well, our camping has mainly been done with families who've had kids growing up and we still have camping even though the kids have grown up. We've vacationed, tried to take, well, a couple of weeks. Cheryl usually tries to take all of June that we can vacation if we want to go someplace. So we've done, when Sue was growing up, have gone off the Black Hills, have had several trips to California down through the Oregon coast and have tried to do things like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Also, a lot of family traveling. Yes. The three of them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because we used to have some cattle too and then we finally decided that you hang, you know, pretty much when we... Since I went back to teaching and Sue brought in school where we had to decide if we're going to have vacation and where we're going to go so we decided we'd give up the cattle and do it with a little bit less money there and still have time to do things together in June and probably July. Because the end of July comes and then you're... You can't go much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So the early part of the summer is really the time for you to take vacation and that's what you and your husband have done together. We continued to do that even after she graduated.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. We still go camping and usually go someplace.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think you made some comparisons. I was going to ask how you compare things now with what you did 30 years ago. I'd say it was, what, 28 years ago when you were married? Mm-hmm. You said you did some canning but can you think of, at that time, think of other comparisons?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think in the cooking end I think I did a lot more baking bread and making desserts and things like that. I enjoyed it but I don't do that anymore. I did more sewing then and I don't now. Dress is different. I think we dress more casually today than we used to because any time you went out it seems like Cheryl always wore the suit, you know, and you dressed up and even with Sue, she reminded me one time when we had gone over to visit my sister and we're coming home and it happened to be on Easter and I had her dressed in a dress to travel and how silly that was, you know, now that we, I think you're more casual that way. More casual. I think we do more, too, today of I'm trying to think of something else. I think at that time then I did my own hair, now I don't. I go to the hairdressers and she's on vacation. That's why I've gone to this type of a hairdo. I can't even do my own hair anymore if you can believe it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You, of course, always had a car so that's not a different thing. Since, I mean, since you've been married. No, no.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We've always had automobiles.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I'd say I'd say that you always had a car, of course, since you were married but then in comparing differences between now and your childhood home and going back even farther than 30 years, you were saying that your mother, of course, had a ringer washer and of course you had a hair dryer.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I have so much more than mother had. It's just she didn't really have very much to work with at all. She always marvelled at everything that I have had because I, just by the appliance you name, I have it. And she just didn't at Christmas buy different appliances in that form and she said that the stove she had there in the apartment where they lived was the nicest stove she'd ever had.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They had a refrigerator?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They had a refrigerator when our sister was born. They got their first refrigerator. We had the icebox and I remember the iceman coming around with his wagon and he was pulled by the two horses and we'd always run out and he'd chip off the ice and you'd grab the ice chips and that was just delicious.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You had electricity.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yes, we had electricity and we had an indoor planning car until we got the icebox done.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: and you said did your parents have a car? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they didn't. Okay. Let's see. We walked every place we went. That's one of the changes that I think when you get cars with me I try to force myself not to walk down after the pavement but so easy just to open the car or something and drive down because we walked to school and had to come home for lunch and that was about a 10 block, 12 block walk. And we thought it wouldn't bother us. Oh, there's another thing with go clear back there but Cheryl has motorcycles and I tried to drive them but I don't like to too well because I don't go very fast but I like to. We have the bigger one and I ride with him on that one so that's fun to do and just to get on those things and take it on. That's another one. So that's another

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know, relaxation or recreation. I don't know, is that relaxing or have you separate areas?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we've never seemed to have too much trouble. I think we talk it over. It was just natural. He's around so much of the time. We always sat down for meals together. We never, I never had to fix one and then another, very seldom. And if Sue was going to be practicing late, we just waited dinner. And he was always here and this was coming up and we just talked things over so that was normal.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that's the way you would handle conflicts. And you said that he often would fix his meals and so on. I was going to ask what was his attitude towards the role of a wife and a woman. He was tolerant?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yes, encouraged I think,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: encouraged me.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If you want to, fine. If you want to do this, fine. It was, never had that feeling that I had to do something in the house first. If there was something else I wanted to do, that was just fine, go ahead and do it. We're individuals, but still we don't go our own ways. I mean, we do things together. But very much so, and the money matters. I probably do all of that. I write all of the checks and everything. And I now and then say, well you should know where this and this is. I said, you know, you may have to do this sometime. But if when it comes to selling the wheat, he does it because he knows how to deal with it. And as a farmer, you always have to borrow from the bank during certain times of the year. And he always done that. I said it would be interesting if I went up to see if they would loan me the money. I've been curious.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, you've been played as a teacher and so on. You've been in the role, the position, and a lot of women are sort of striving for debt. What do you think about the changing role of women?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I like to see them become fair. I know we still have friends who, she's never worked. And I begin to see it in their own kids, that girls, they don't want to work for them after they get married. Some find it's a necessity and have gone to work. But to me, I don't know how you could just sit at home if you didn't have children right away, how you would occupy your time. I think it's nice, but I think you have to get around with adults too. Our daughter has mentioned she doesn't have a job yet and she's hoping to get one because she wants to work before they start a family. And when she first moved over there and before school started, she just about went crazy because she didn't have adult people to talk to. It was a new neighborhood. I think that's the way I'd be. And so many say...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So she really wants to work. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And once in a while we'll have arguments, no matter, you might say arguments, but they say, well, I want my meals, I want big meals. And I'd say, well, that really isn't that necessary all the time. It's something we can't,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: maybe they do it just to argue.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I say, well, I'm going to pack up to camp. If I'm busy, I tell everybody to go Sue and Cheryl and get your own things packed and ready to go. Maybe if I had the time, I could check them over and make sure they had everything. But everybody's kind of responsible for their own stuff. But then I can see, if I wasn't this one class a day, but I'm working right up until we go and she's home all the time. That's why I expect her to pack for me. I expect her to do things that I think are not too necessary. And I still see it, and I said, it never worked.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You're not speaking of how it works in your home,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: but how it works with friends. No, but it never has. No, I've probably had the night and see that some are striving for, because I know that there are children that go to school and they talk to me and I know that their mothers have quite a rough time. And I can tell everybody at all times, and be there to wait on them. Well, I didn't even see that with my own folks, you see. So, I've never seen that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You've grown up in an atmosphere where that situation, that the mother is just the servant and hasn't really

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I think my mother-in-law, she was more to, she was always home to cook and she didn't go very much. speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, very large. You know, and didn't have her. We've talked some about the small town. speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right now, no. I think, I don't know. With the young people for her that stayed around here, she said their entertainment seems mainly, from those that seem to be living here now, that grew up and living here now that are her age, are married, that their whole entertainment is just Saturday night with the bar. And she said, there's so much more than that. Now, she was looking at just a few of them and I don't know if maybe, there's a lot of different things and there's different things that they do over there. But I said to her, I said, well, not everyone does. We don't. We go other places too. But I think she was referring to her own friends that are still around. Now, if they would come back to this area, I think they would take advantage of Moscow and Poland and Spokane like we do. But she felt that they're just geared one way with the beer bus. And although she was with these same kids and did some of the same things that he did in school, she felt that she didn't want to stay around this whole town. And I think it was the social life, the activity that she had. But you have to go and, if you're not just going to be with any young person, you'd have to tell them that they would have to find their activity if they didn't just want to go to the bar Saturday night. But you can do it. But you can't sit at home. A small town is also hard. A new person coming into a small town has their problems too because people don't always flock to them. You think, you know, you do, oh, there's a new person, you'll go see them. But you might go visit them once and then you know you don't go back again. And I have found that some of the people, when they first moved in here, they had a very difficult time getting acquainted. But the thing to do is to get involved, if you want to, in some of the organizations that are around, the new church or something. You have to go out and look for.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Nobody's living in, moving to a small town or in a rural area to become involved.

speaker: Speaker 1

Then, Don, after living there or being there a couple years going to school, that, gee, if I want to get this job I'll get it. So he came back here and went to work in Moscow at a garage. words: But he really did make sort of a conscious decision to come back to a smaller town. Moscow. A lot smaller than the big city. I guess, well, let's see. speaker: Speaker 1
words: You do both of those.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I think being around with with family fulfilling was to me, too, when I got my master's degree. And I'm glad that I could do it. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Developed your home together and enjoy. Mm-hmm. Beautiful home. Is there anything else that you think you might have said or would like to tell me about the experiences of a woman in a rural area?

words: You had said earlier that you were glad that you raised your daughter in a small town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And I suppose...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm not afraid of any of the students high school or otherwise. Because we don't have in any way in this area it doesn't seem... Although we're getting people that I might question, you know. speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think that that...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I think that helps with children if you realize oh hey, he's tired today and he can't function today. Well, you know that mom and dad maybe drink a lot and mom has different ones living with her. And things get pretty rough at home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you would say that helps with the students who have problems as well as with

speaker: Speaker 2
words: good students. Because I find sometimes with new teachers they get real uptight about this and they can't understand why they can't do this and this. I say well they're doing pretty well with what they had to work with. Well if you explain what kind of home life they have then they begin to say well yes I'll be more tolerant of this and try and do my understanding. And that's what it takes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This is really quite a change. Have you ever used that area as a recreation area? Have people ever gone up there for picnics or anything like that?

words: Have you ever known any people who've lived up there?

words: I suppose, well, on some of those roads I suppose there are some children who come into it.

words: Oh, really?
